..
Issued at 250 AM CDT Sat Oct 24 2026

Slow-moving band of rain showers is exiting eastward across western 
WI, with a more recent batch trailing showers captured on radar over 
portions of central MN. These showers have developed within a 40-
50kt LLJ that spans from SW to NE across MN. Not anticipating these 
showers to be too heavy as latest ACARS data along with forecast 
soundings depict a very dry lowest 10k feet of the column along 
with a lack of elevated instability. Breezy southeasterly surface 
flow combined with cloud cover is working to limit cooling, so 
morning lows are on track to only dip into the upper 50s to lower 
60s (this is ~5-7 degrees warmer than normal highs this late in 
October!). 

One more warm day ahead, as the Upper Midwest begins the day 
located within the warm sector of a deepening surface cyclone 
positioned over south central Canada. The system is progged to 
rapidly lift northeast through the day and will send a trailing 
cold front southeastward across the forecast area. The front is 
progged to be near the border of the Dakotas and MN by daybreak,
where showers and a few rumbles of thunder will be possible through
the morning. The morning frontal position sets the stage for a 
10+ degree high temperature gradient from western MN to western
WI. The earlier frontal passage across western MN will limit 
heating and support highs in the lower 60s. Surface heating is 
forecast to be more efficient through the morning and into the 
early afternoon to the east of the front over much of east- 
central and southeastern MN as well as western WI. Filtered 
sunshine and ongoing WAA will yield highs in the low to mid 70s 
for locations that remain east of the front through midday. The 
band of rain showers will move east towards the I-35 corridor 
this afternoon and continue to drift eastward through the 
evening. Rainfall amounts will be the greatest across western MN
(isolated tenth to quarter inch amounts possible) and decrease 
with eastward movement through the day (a few hundredths across 
southeastern MN/western WI). Winds turn northwesterly behind the
frontal passage and will usher in much cooler air for Sunday. 
Forecast highs fall to more seasonal levels in the low to mid 
50s. The mostly cloudy and cooler Sunday weather will also 
feature the potential for a few isolated raindrops. 

Better chances for widespread rain (particularly across the western 
half of the forecast area) will arrive early in the work week as a 
compact upper-level shortwave lifts north through the Plains. 
Associated surface low is forecast to develop and track from 
central NE to northwestern MN Monday into Tuesday. This 
evolution will combine with PWATs 200-250% of normal to support 
a shield of heavy precipitation along the surface low track. A 
swath of 1-1.5" rainfall amounts appears most likely along the 
consensus low track from central NE to eastern SD into far 
western MN. While most communities will observe rain, overall 
amounts will lower as one moves east from far western MN. 
Continued cloud cover and rain spreading north results in cooler
highs in the 40s across much of central/western MN on Monday.

The aforementioned upper-level shortwave is progged to shear out 
near the International Border as a more potent trailing wave digs 
across the northern CONUS Tuesday into Wednesday. This will spawn a 
surface cyclone near the International Border, once again placing
the Upper Midwest on the "warm side" of the system. Temperatures
should rebound into the 50s/60s on Tuesday prior to the passage
of another front late Tuesday into Wednesday morning. Guidance 
varies on the timing and coverage of precipitation during this 
period, but the 30-50% PoPs early in the day on Wednesday tend 
to represent the forecast uncertainties well at this distance. 
Our latest forecast shows highs in the low to mid 60s following 
the early morning precipitation on Wednesday. We'll note that 
these temperatures may be too warm should the timing and 
evolution of upper-level and surface features slow down in 
upcoming forecasts. 

The second half of next week features a return to large scale 
ridging over central CONUS, however influence from an active 
southwesterly jet may support occasional rain chances. In 
addition, the ridging is fueling a growing number of ensemble 
members (including machine learning ensemble counterparts) that 
feature a return to above normal temperatures heading into 
Halloween weekend. Should this become more of a "trend" we could
see the NBM warm out of the upper 50s (which is already above 
normal) late next week.
